THOUGHT: This 72-year-old male presents with classic “B symptoms”-like systemic features—fatigue and unintentional weight loss (5 kg over 6 months)—despite preserved appetite, which raises concern for an underlying malignancy or chronic inflammatory condition. Notably, he has no fever or night sweats, making classic lymphoma B symptoms incomplete, but the physical exam is highly revealing: diffuse, nontender lymphadenopathy + hepatosplenomegaly + left and right upper quadrant dullness (consistent with splenomegaly and hepatomegaly). Lab findings show lymphocytosis (WBC 16,000/μL), mild normocytic anemia (Hb 11 g/dL), and a positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT), indicating autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA). The peripheral smear shows increased lymphocytes with smudge cells — a hallmark of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). Smudge cells result from fragile malignant B lymphocytes rupturing during slide preparation. CLL is the most common adult leukemia in Western countries, typically diagnosed in older adults (median age ~70), and frequently presents with asymptomatic lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy, and/or organomegaly. AIHA occurs in ~10–25% of CLL patients and explains the positive DAT and anemia. The combination of age, lymphocytosis with smudge cells, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and AIHA strongly points to CLL — not reactive lymphocytosis (which would lack smudge cells and organomegaly), not mantle cell or follicular lymphoma (less likely to present with prominent smudge cells or DAT+ AIHA), and not acute leukemia (no blasts on smear, normal platelets, indolent course). Further workup (e.g., flow cytometry showing CD5+/CD23+/CD19+/CD20dim clonal B cells) would confirm, but clinical and morphologic findings are diagnostic.

DIAGNOSIS: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia
